paras: The lynching of Frank and John McDonald was the killing of two cousins by a mob at Menominee, Michigan, on the night of September 27, 1881, after they had been jailed on a charge of fatally stabbing a young man named Willie Kittson. A crowd that reports put at 400 to more than 500 people overpowered the sheriff, broke into the county jail and dragged the two men to their deaths. Wire summaries carried the story across the country in early October, and a Wisconsin paper later reported the arrest of members of the lynching party.

According to a dispatch from Menominee dated September 28, Frank and John McDonald were ex-convicts who had finished an eighteen-month term in the state prison only two weeks earlier. A shorter wire summary said they had served two years in the penitentiary and had come back "for vengeance." The Eaton Democrat called them "desperate characters," but a special dispatch to the Chicago Daily Tribune said the cousins had borne good characters in their home city.

The Menominee account said the cousins got into a row with Willie Kittson, described as "a half-breed" about 23 years old, at a "disreputable house" on the outskirts of the village. When Norman Kittson and Tommy Dunn took Willie away, the McDonalds attacked them in the street; Willie was stabbed and died within minutes, and Norman was wounded so badly he was not expected to live. Sheriff Barclay arrested the cousins and lodged them in the county jail, where extra guards were posted as excitement grew.

About 10 o'clock the next night a mob of over 500, "composed mostly of Frenchmen, Indians and half-breeds," overpowered the sheriff and guard and broke open the jail with timbers, sledgehammers and axes. The prisoners were dragged by ropes around their necks three-quarters of a mile to the house where the row had begun, and their bodies were hung from a tree. The dispatch said the men were dead "long before" they were hung up, and that the mob then set the house on fire and burned it to the ground. Citizens who answered the sheriff's call came too late, and the authorities took the bodies down the next morning.

On October 22 the Superior Times, in its column of state news, reported that a number of the lynching party had been arrested, among them the "ringleader, Forvilly." The item said the father of one of the men, reportedly worth about $300,000, and a brother of the elder McDonald were pressing for justice. No report of an inquest, indictment or trial appears in the coverage. On November 5 the paper added that one of the two cousins had in fact been named McDougall rather than McDonald.

At least three separate wire versions circulated. An Oconto, Wisconsin, telegram in the Cheyenne Daily Leader on October 2 called the cousins "two roughs" who had "brutally murdered" two Kitson brothers; the Wellington Enterprise repeated it, and the South Kentuckian garbled it into a lynching at Oconto. A second summary, in the Wheeling Register, the Ottawa Free Trader and the Watertown Republican, presented the stabbing as revenge by released convicts; the Free Trader headed it "VENGEANCE!" and wrote that they returned "for vengeance, and got it!"

The full Menominee dispatch, headed "Murder and Lynch Law," ran in the Crawford Avalanche of Grayling, Michigan, and the Kenosha Telegraph. It set the crime and the lynching side by side without comment, though it said the prisoners were dragged "mercilessly" through the street. Several reports called the Kittsons and much of the mob "half-breeds" or Indians, but none stated the race of the McDonalds.

Reports differed on the alleged crime: the Oconto telegram and the Eaton Democrat said two Kitson brothers were murdered, while the fuller accounts said one was killed and the other fatally wounded. Accounts of the deaths also varied, from men dragged to death and hung up afterward in the two fuller versions to the Eaton Democrat's statement that the mob "clubbed, shot and hanged them." The Eaton Democrat dated the stabbing to the 24th, and the Superior Times placed the lynching at Marinette, while the dispatch from the scene was datelined Menominee, Michigan.

reader.title: Lynching of Frank and John McDonald
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A mob broke into a county jail, took two men held on a murder charge and killed them (A9, A1, A7).

A mob of 400 to over 500 overpowered the sheriff and guard, took two prisoners accused of a fatal stabbing from the jail and killed them, presented as retribution for the crime (A9, A1, A10). The race of the two men is never stated, so whether this is an anti-Black lynching is not supported by the papers (see flags).

Separate wire versions (the Menominee dispatch A9, the 'vengeance' summary A1, the Oconto telegram A3, and a Canadian dispatch A11) agree that two McDonald cousins jailed for killing a Kittson were taken from jail and lynched by a mob.

accounts.label: Oconto telegram

accounts.label: Canadian dispatch to the Chicago Tribune
accounts.gist: John and Frank McDonald of the dispatch's city, arrested for killing a man in a row, were taken from jail and hanged at Menominee; they had borne good characters there.

accounts.label: Wisconsin state-news column
accounts.gist: Places the lynching at Marinette; reports arrests of lynchers and a later correction of one victim's name to McDougall.

framing.detail: Headed 'Murder and Lynch Law'; reports the crime and the lynching in sequence without editorial comment, though it says the prisoners were dragged 'mercilessly'.
The Ottawa Free Trader headed the summary 'VENGEANCE!' and said the McDonalds returned 'for vengeance, and got it!'
Brief items call the cousins 'two roughs' who 'brutally murdered' the Kitsons, or 'desperate characters', and report the lynching flatly.
A Canadian dispatch notes the men 'bore good characters' at home, a counterweight to the 'roughs' framing.
